{{Short description|Mathematical structure}}
A '''sparsity matroid''' is a [[mathematical structure]] that captures how densely a [[multigraph]] is populated with edges.  To unpack this a little, sparsity is a measure of [[Dense graph|density of a graph]] that bounds the number of edges in any subgraph. The property of having a particular matroid as its density measure is invariant under graph isomorphisms and so it is a [[graph invariant]].

The graphs we are concerned with generalise simple [[directed graph]]s by allowing multiple same-oriented edges between pairs of vertices. [[Matroids]] are a quite general mathematical abstraction that describe the amount of indepdendence in, variously, points in geometric space and paths in a graph; when applied to characterising sparsity, matroids describe certain sets of sparse graphs.  These matroids are connected to the [[structural rigidity]] of graphs and their ability to be decomposed into edge-disjoint [[spanning tree]]s via the Tutte and [[Nash-Williams theorem]].  There is a family of efficient algorithms, known as [[pebble game]]s, for determining if a multigraph meets the given sparsity condition.

== Definitions ==
'''<math>(k,l)</math>-sparse multigraph.''' <ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|date=2008-04-28|title=Pebble game algorithms and sparse graphs|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012365X07005602|journal=Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=308|issue=8|pages=1425–1437|doi=10.1016/j.disc.2007.07.104|issn=0012-365X|last1=Lee |first1=Audrey |last2=Streinu |first2=Ileana |s2cid=2826 |arxiv=math/0702129}}</ref>  A multigraph <math>G=(V,E)</math> is <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse, where <math>k</math> and <math>l</math> are non-negative integers, if for every subgraph <math>G'=(V',E')</math> of <math>G</math>, we have <math>|E'| \leq k|V'| - l</math>.

'''<math>(k,l)</math>-tight multigraph.''' <ref name=":0" />  A multigraph <math>G=(V,E)</math> is <math>(k,l)</math>-tight if it is <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse and <math>|E|=k|V|-l</math>.

'''<math>[a,b]</math>-sparse and tight multigraph.''' <ref>{{Cite journal|date=2012-10-01|title=Body-and-cad geometric constraint systems|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925772112000235|journal=Computational Geometry|language=en|volume=45|issue=8|pages=385–405|doi=10.1016/j.comgeo.2010.06.003|issn=0925-7721|last1=Haller |first1=Kirk |last2=Lee-St.John |first2=Audrey |last3=Sitharam |first3=Meera |last4=Streinu |first4=Ileana |last5=White |first5=Neil |arxiv=1006.1126}}</ref>  A multigraph <math>G=(V,E \cup F)</math> is <math>[a,b]</math>-sparse if there exists a subset <math>F' \subset F</math> such that the subgraph <math>G'=(V,E \cup F')</math> is <math>(a,a)</math>-sparse and the subgraph <math>G'' =(V,F \setminus F')</math> is <math>(b,b)</math>-sparse.  The multigraph <math>G</math> is <math>[a,b]</math>-tight if, additionally, <math>|E \cup F| = (a+b)|V|-(a+b)</math>.

'''<math>(k,l)</math>-sparsity matroid.''' <ref name=":0" />  The <math>(k,l)</math>-sparsity matroid is a matroid whose ground set is the edge set of the complete multigraph on <math>n</math> vertices, with loop multiplicity <math>k-l</math> and edge multiplicity <math>2k-l</math>, and whose independent sets are <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse multigraphs on <math>n</math> vertices.  The bases of the matroid are the <math>(k,l)</math>-tight multigraphs and the circuits are the <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse multigraphs <math>G=(V,E)</math> that satisfy <math>|E|=k|V|-l+1</math>.

The first examples of sparsity matroids can be found in.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lorea|first=M.|date=1979-01-01|title=On matroidal families|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X%2879%2990190-0|journal=Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=28|issue=1|pages=103–106|doi=10.1016/0012-365X(79)90190-0|issn=0012-365X|doi-access=free}}</ref>  Not all pairs <math>(k,l)</math> induce a matroid.

== Pairs (k,l) that form a matroid ==
The following result provides sufficient restrictions on <math>(k,l)</math> for the existence of a matroid.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":0" />  The <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse multigraphs on <math>n</math> vertices are the independent sets of a matroid if

* <math>n \geq 1</math> and <math>l \in [0,k]</math>;
* <math>n \geq 2</math> and <math>l \in (k,\frac{3}{2}k)</math>; or
* <math>n = 2</math> or <math>n \geq \frac{l}{2k-l}</math> and <math>l \in [\frac{3}{2}k,2k)</math>.

Some consequences of this theorem are that <math>(2,3)</math>-sparse multigraphs form a matroid while <math>(3,6)</math>-sparse multigraphs do not.  Hence, the bases, i.e., <math>(2,3)</math>-tight multigraphs, must all have the same number of edges and can be constructed using techniques discussed below.  On the other hand, without this matroidal structure, maximally <math>(3,6)</math>-sparse multigraphs will have different numbers of edges, and it is interesting to identify the one with the maximum number of edges.

== Connections to rigidity and decomposition ==
Structural rigidity is about determining if almost all, i.e. [[Generic property|generic]], [[Graph embedding|embeddings]] of a (simple or multi) graph in some <math>d</math>-dimensional [[metric space]] are rigid.  More precisely, this theory gives combinatorial characterizations of such graphs.  In [[Euclidean space]], [[James Clerk Maxwell|Maxwell]] showed that independence in a sparsity matroid is necessary for a graph to be generically rigid in any dimension.

'''Maxwell Direction.''' <ref>{{Cite journal|last=F.R.S|first=J. Clerk Maxwell|date=1864-04-01|title=XLV. On reciprocal figures and diagrams of forces|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/14786446408643663|journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science|volume=27|issue=182|pages=250–261|doi=10.1080/14786446408643663|issn=1941-5982|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  If a graph <math>G</math> is generically minimally rigid in <math>d</math>-dimensions, then it is independent in the <math>\left(d,{d+1 \choose 2}\right)</math>-sparsity matroid.

The converse of this theorem was proved in <math>2</math>-dimensions, yielding a complete combinatorial characterization of generically rigid graphs in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>.  However, the converse is not true for <math>d \geq 3</math>, see [[Structural rigidity#Combinatorial characterizations of generically rigid graphs|combinatorial characterizations of generically rigid graphs]].

Other sparsity matroids have been used to give combinatorial characterizations of generically rigid multigraphs for various types of frameworks, see [[Structural rigidity#Rigidity for other types of frameworks|rigidity for other types of frameworks]].  The following table summarizes these results by stating the type of generic rigid framework in a given dimension and the equivalent sparsity condition.  Let <math>kG</math> be the multigraph obtained by duplicating the edges of a multigraph <math>G</math> <math>k</math> times.

The Tutte and Nash-Williams theorem shows that <math>(k,k)</math>-tight graphs are equivalent to graphs that can be decomposed into <math>k</math> edge-disjoint spanning trees, called <math>k</math>-arborescences.  A <math>(k,a)</math>-arborescence is a multigraph <math>G</math> such that adding <math>a</math> edges to <math>G</math> yields a <math>k</math>-arborescence.  For <math>l \in [k,2k)</math>, a <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse multigraph is a <math>(k,l-k)</math>-arborescence;<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Haas|first=Ruth|date=2002|title=Characterizations of arboricity of graphs|url=|journal=Ars Combinatoria|volume=63|pages=|via=}}</ref> this was first shown for <math>(2,3)</math> sparse graphs.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lovász|first1=L.|last2=Yemini|first2=Y.|date=1982-03-01|title=On Generic Rigidity in the Plane|url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0603009|journal=SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods|volume=3|issue=1|pages=91–98|doi=10.1137/0603009|issn=0196-5212|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Recski|first=András|date=1984-03-01|title=A network theory approach to the rigidity of skeletal structures Part I. Modelling and interconnection|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0166-218X%2884%2990007-6|journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics|language=en|volume=7|issue=3|pages=313–324|doi=10.1016/0166-218X(84)90007-6|issn=0166-218X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  Additionally, many of the rigidity and sparsity results above can be written in terms of edge-disjoint spanning trees.

== Constructing sparse multigraphs ==
This section gives methods to construct various sparse multigraphs using operations defined in [[Structural rigidity#Constructing generically rigid graphs|constructing generically rigid graphs]].  Since these operations are defined for a given dimension, let a <math>(k,0)</math>-extension be a <math>k</math>-dimensional <math>0</math>-extension, i.e., a <math>0</math>-extension where the new vertex is connected to <math>k</math> distinct vertices.  Likewise, a <math>(k,1)</math>-extension is a <math>k</math>-dimensional <math>1</math>-extension.

== General (k,l)-sparse multigraphs ==
The first construction is for <math>\left(k,k\right)</math>-tight graphs.  A generalized <math>(k,1)</math>-extension is a triple <math>(k,1,j)</math>, where <math>j</math> edges are removed, for <math>1 \leq j \leq k</math>, and the new vertex <math>u</math> is connected to the vertices of these <math>j</math> edges and to <math>k - j</math> distinct vertices.  The usual <math>(k,1)</math>-extension is a <math>(k,1,1)</math>-extension.

'''Theorem.''' <ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tay|first=Tiong-Seng|date=1991|title=Henneberg's Method for Bar and Body Frameworks|journal=Structural Topology|url=https://upcommons.upc.edu/handle/2099/1066|issn=0226-9171}}</ref>  A multigraph is <math>(k,k)</math>-tight [[if and only if]] it can be constructed from a single vertex via a sequence of <math>(k,0)</math>- and <math>(k,1,j)</math>-extensions.

This theorem was then extended to general <math>(k,l)</math>-tight graphs.  Consider another generalization of a <math>1</math>-extension denoted by <math>(k,1,i,j)</math>, for <math>0 \leq j \leq i \leq k</math>, where <math>j</math> edges are removed, the new vertex <math>u</math> is connected to the vertices of these <math>j</math> edges, <math>i-j</math> loops are added to <math>u</math>, and <math>u</math> is connected to <math>k-i</math> other distinct vertices.  Also, let <math>P_l</math> denote a multigraph with a single node and <math>l</math> loops.

'''Theorem.''' <ref>{{Citation|last1=Fekete|first1=Zsolt|chapter=A Note on [k, l]-sparse Graphs|date=2007|chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-7643-7400-6_13|title=Graph Theory in Paris: Proceedings of a Conference in Memory of Claude Berge|pages=169–177|editor-last=Bondy|editor-first=Adrian|series=Trends in Mathematics|place=Basel|publisher=Birkhäuser|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-7643-7400-6_13|isbn=978-3-7643-7400-6|access-date=2021-01-22|last2=Szegő|first2=László|editor2-last=Fonlupt|editor2-first=Jean|editor3-last=Fouquet|editor3-first=Jean-Luc|editor4-last=Fournier|editor4-first=Jean-Claude|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>  A multigraph <math>G</math> is <math>(k,l)</math>-tight for

* <math>l \in [1,k]</math> if and only if <math>G</math> can be constructed from <math>P_{k-l}</math> via a sequence of <math>(k,1,i,j)</math>-extensions, such that <math>0 \leq j \leq i \leq k-1</math> and <math>i-j \leq k-l</math>;
* <math>l=0</math> if and only if <math>G</math> can be constructed from <math>P_{k-l}</math> via a sequence of <math>(k,1,i,j)</math>-extensions, such that <math>0 \leq j \leq i \leq k</math> and <math>i-j \leq k-l</math>.

Neither of these constructions are sufficient when the graph is simple.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|date=2014-11-01|title=A constructive characterisation of circuits in the simple (2,2)-sparsity matroid|journal=[[European Journal of Combinatorics]]|language=en|volume=42|pages=92–106|doi=10.1016/j.ejc.2014.05.009|doi-access=free|issn=0195-6698|last1=Nixon |first1=Anthony |s2cid=1419117 }}</ref>  The next results are for <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse [[hypergraph]]s.  A hypergraph is <math>s</math>-uniform if each of its edges contains exactly <math>s</math> vertices.  First, conditions are established for the existence of <math>(k,l)</math>-tight hypergraphs.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|date=2009-11-01|title=Sparse hypergraphs and pebble game algorithms|journal=[[European Journal of Combinatorics]]|language=en|volume=30|issue=8|pages=1944–1964|doi=10.1016/j.ejc.2008.12.018|doi-access=free|issn=0195-6698|last1=Streinu |first1=Ileana |last2=Theran |first2=Louis |s2cid=5477763 }}</ref>  There exists an <math>n_0</math> such that for all <math>n \geq n_0</math>, there exist <math>s</math>-uniform hypergraphs on <math>n</math> vertices that are <math>(k,l)</math>-tight.

The next result extends the Tutte and Nash-Williams theorem to hypergraphs.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":6" />  If <math>G</math> is a <math>(k,l)</math>-tight hypergraph, for <math>l \geq k</math>, then <math>G</math> is a <math>(k,l-k)</math> arborescence, where the <math>l-k</math> added edges contain at least two vertices.

A map-hypergraph is a hypergraph that admits an [[Orientation (graph theory)|orientation]] such that each vertex has an out-degree of <math>1</math>.  A <math>k</math>-map-hypergraph is a map-hypergraph that can be decomposed into <math>k</math> edge-disjoint map-hypergraphs.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":6" />  If <math>G</math> is a <math>(k,l)</math>-tight hypergraph, for <math>k \geq l</math>, then <math>g</math> is the union of an <math>l</math>-arborescence and a <math>(k-l)</math>-map-hypergraph.

== (2,3)-sparse graphs ==
[[File:2-3 circuit.jpg|thumb|203x203px|'''Figure 1.''' A <math>(2,3)</math>-circuit.]]
The first result shows that <math>(2,3)</math>-tight graphs, i.e., generically minimally rigid graphs in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> have Henneberg-constructions.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Citation|last=Henneberg|first=I.|chapter=Die Graphische Statik der Starren Körper|date=1908|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-3-663-16021-2_5|title=Encyklopädie der Mathematischen Wissenschaften mit Einschluss ihrer Anwendungen|pages=345–434|place=Wiesbaden|publisher=Vieweg+Teubner Verlag|doi=10.1007/978-3-663-16021-2_5 |isbn=978-3-663-15450-1|access-date=2021-01-22|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>  A graph <math>G</math> is <math>(2,3)</math>-tight if and only if it can be constructed from the complete graph <math>K_2</math> via a sequence of <math>0</math>- and <math>1</math>-extensions.

The next result shows how to construct <math>(2,3)</math>-circuits.  In this setting, a [[Clique-sum|<math>2</math>-sum]] combines two graphs by identifying two <math>K_2</math> subgraphs in each and then removing the combined edge from the resulting graph.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|date=2003-05-01|title=A proof of Connelly's conjecture on 3-connected circuits of the rigidity matroid|journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]| series=Series B|language=en|volume=88|issue=1|pages=77–97|doi=10.1016/S0095-8956(02)00037-0|doi-access=free|issn=0095-8956|last1=Berg |first1=Alex R. |last2=Jordán |first2=Tibor }}</ref>  A graph <math>G</math> is a <math>(2,3)</math>-circuit if and only if it can be constructed from disjoint copies of the complete graph <math>K_4</math> via a sequence of <math>1</math>-extensions within connected components and <math>2</math>-sums of connected components.

The method for constructing <math>3</math>-connected <math>(2,3)</math>-circuits is even simpler.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":7" />  A graph <math>G</math> is a <math>3</math>-connected <math>(2,3)</math>-circuit if and only if it can be constructed from the complete graph <math>K_4</math> via a sequence of <math>1</math>-extensions.

These circuits also have the following combinatorial property.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":7" />  If a graph <math>G</math> is a <math>(2,3)</math>-circuit that is not the complete graph <math>K_4</math>, then <math>G</math> has at least <math>3</math> vertices of degree <math>3</math> such that performing a <math>1</math>-reduction on any one of these vertices yields another <math>(2,3)</math>-circuit.

== (2,2)-sparse graphs ==
The next results shows how to construct <math>(2,2)</math>-circuits using two different construction methods.  For the first method, the base graphs are shown in Figure 2 and the three join operations are shows in Figure 2.  A <math>1</math>-join identifies a <math>K_2</math> subgraph in <math>G_1</math> with an edge of a <math>K_4</math> subgraph in <math>G_1</math>, and removes the other two vertices of the <math>K_4</math>.  A <math>2</math>-join identifies an edge of a <math>K_4</math> subgraph in <math>G_1</math> with an edge of a <math>K_4</math> subgraph in <math>G_2</math>, and removes the other vertices on both <math>K_4</math> subgraphs.  A <math>3</math>-join takes a degree <math>3</math> vertex <math>v_1</math> in <math>G_1</math> and a degree <math>3</math> vertex <math>v_2</math> in <math>G_2</math> and removes them, then it adds <math>3</math> edges between <math>G_1</math> and <math>G_2</math> such that there is a [[bijection]] between the neighbors of <math>v_1</math> and <math>v_2</math>.
[[File:2-2 base.jpg|center|thumb|440x440px|'''Figure 2.'''  The base graphs for constructing <math>(2,2)</math>-circuits.]]
[[File:2-2 joins.jpg|center|thumb|300x300px|'''Figure 3.'''  From top to bottom, the <math>1</math>-, <math>2</math>-, and <math>3</math>-join operations for constructing <math>(2,2)</math>-circuits.]]
The second method uses <math>2</math>-dimensional vertex-splitting, defined in the [[Structural rigidity#Constructing generically rigid graphs|constructing generically rigid graphs]], and a vertex-to-<math>K_4</math> operation, which replace a vertex <math>v</math> of a graph with a <math>K_4</math> graph and connects each neighbor of <math>v</math> to any vertex of the <math>K_4</math>.
'''Theorem.'''  A graph <math>G</math> is a <math>(2,2)</math>-circuit if and only if
* <math>G</math> can be constructed from disjoint copies of the base graphs via a sequence of <math>1</math>-extensions within connected components and <math>1</math>-, <math>2</math>-, and <math>3</math>- sums of connected components;<ref name=":5" />
* [[File:2-2 circuit.jpg|thumb|'''Figure 4.''' A <math>(2,2)</math>-circuit.]]<math>G</math> can be constructed from <math>K_4</math> via a sequence of <math>0</math>- and <math>1</math>-extensions, vertex-to-<math>K_4</math>, and <math>2</math>-dimensional vertex-splitting operations<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last1=Nixon|first1=Anthony|last2=Owen|first2=John|date=2014-12-30|title=An inductive construction of $(2,1)$-tight graphs|url=https://cdm.ucalgary.ca/article/view/62096|journal=Contributions to Discrete Mathematics|language=en|volume=9|issue=2|doi=10.11575/cdm.v9i2.62096|s2cid=35739977 |issn=1715-0868}}</ref>

== (2,1)-sparse graphs ==
The following result gives a construction method for <math>(2,1)</math>-tight graphs and extends the Tutte and Nash-Williams theorem to these graphs.  For the construction, the base graphs are <math>K_5</math> with an edge removed or the <math>2</math>-sum of two <math>K_4</math> graphs (the shared edge is not removed), see the middle graph in Figure 2.  Also, an edge-joining operation adds a single edge between two graphs.

'''Theorem.''' <ref name=":8" />  A graph <math>G</math> is <math>(2,1)</math>-tight if and only if

* <math>G</math> can be obtained from <math>K_5</math> with an edge removed or the <math>2</math>-sum of two <math>K_4</math> graphs via a sequence of <math>0</math>- and <math>1</math>-extensions, vertex-to-<math>K_4</math>, <math>2</math>-dimensional vertex-splitting, and edge-joining operations;
* <math>G</math> is the edge-disjoint union of a spanning tree and a spanning graph in which every connected component contains exactly one cycle.

== Pebble games ==
There is a family of efficient network-flow based algorithms for identifying <math>(k,l)</math>-sparse graphs, where <math>l \in [0,2k]</math>.<ref name=":0" />  The first of these types of algorithms was for <math>(2,3)</math>-sparse graphs.  These algorithms are explained on the Pebble game page.
